How long humans have lived in the Americas
column2: Native American history reaches back at least 15,000 years to the last Ice Age, when nomadic hunters from Asia first entered the Americas.

column1: When Beringia formed a land bridge
column2: Between about 25,000 and 15,000 BP, falling sea levels exposed Beringia between Siberia and Alaska, creating a possible migration route into the Americas.

column1: When people lived at Monte Verde, Chile
column2: The Monte Verde campsite in Chile dates to about 14,600 BP, which is older than the earliest accepted Clovis evidence in North America.

column1: When the Buttermilk Creek tools were made
column2: Stone tools found beneath Clovis layers at Buttermilk Creek, Texas, date to about 15,500 BP, giving strong evidence that people arrived before the Clovis culture.

column1: When the Folsom site was dated
column2: Radiocarbon tests dated the Folsom bison kill site in New Mexico to about 10,800 BP, confirming that humans hunted in Ice Age America.

column1: When genetic research showed three migrations
column2: In 2012 a major whole-genome study reported evidence for three separate migrations from Siberia into the Americas, supporting the multiple-migration theory.

column1: When distinctive regional cultures developed
column2: Between 10,000 and 2,500 years ago, peoples across the Americas adapted to changing post-Ice Age environments and formed distinctive regional cultures.

column1: When the agricultural revolution began in Mesoamerica
column2: About 9,000 years ago, Mesoamerican peoples began domesticating plants, starting the agricultural revolution of the Western Hemisphere.

column1: When farming spread to the Southwest
column2: By 1000 BCE farming had spread northward from Mesoamerica to the Southwest, roughly a thousand years after Southeastern peoples began cultivating gourds and pumpkins.

column1: When Southeastern peoples began farming
column2: Around 2000 BCE some Southeastern groups began to cultivate gourds and pumpkins, and later maize, adding farming to their hunting and gathering.

column1: When Mayan civilization was at its height
column2: Between the third and ninth centuries CE, Mayan civilization flourished in about fifty urban centers across the Yucatán and neighboring lands.

column1: When ballplayers began scoring through stone rings
column2: After about 800 CE, Mesoamerican ballplayers could score by sending a heavy rubber ball through a stone ring set high on the court wall.

column1: When the Mayan political order collapsed
column2: By about 900 CE the Mayan political order had collapsed, though scholars still debate whether war, ecology, or resource strain caused the collapse.

column1: When the Adena and Hopewell built burial mounds
column2: About 2,000 years ago, Adena and Hopewell communities built burial mounds in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys and filled them with imported prestige goods.

column1: When the Anasazi population peaked
column2: Between about 900 and 1100 CE, the Anasazi population reached its peak of about 30,000 people spread across a vast area of the Southwest.

column1: When Cahokia reached its height
column2: By the twelfth century CE, Cahokia had become the leading city-building and trading center of eastern North America.

column1: How many people lived at Cahokia
column2: At its height, Cahokia may have held as many as 30,000 people, making Cahokia one of the largest cities in North America before European contact.

column1: When the Aztecs arrived in central Mexico
column2: In the mid-thirteenth century, the Aztecs migrated south from northern Mesoamerica and settled in the Valley of Mexico in central Mexico.

column1: When the Aztec empire peaked
column2: By the late fifteenth century, the Aztecs ruled a large tribute empire centered on their island capital of Tenochtitlán.

column1: How many people lived in Tenochtitlán
column2: By the late fifteenth century, Tenochtitlán may have housed about a quarter of a million people, making the Aztec capital a major world city.

column1: When many American cultures declined
column2: During the three to four hundred years before Europeans arrived, many sophisticated American cultures declined sharply or disappeared for reasons that remain a mystery.

column1: When lasting European contact began
column2: In 1492 Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean, beginning lasting contact that would devastate Native peoples through disease and conquest.

column1: How many people lived in North America and the Caribbean by 1492
column2: Somewhere between 57 and 112 million people lived in over 350 different societies in North America and the Caribbean when Europeans arrived.

column1: What share of the world's crops came from the Americas
column2: Plants domesticated by Native Americans, including corn, squash, potatoes, and beans, today account for three-fifths of the world's crops.

column1: How many large mammals humans domesticated worldwide
column2: Of 148 large mammal species worldwide, humans domesticated only fourteen before the twentieth century, so few wild animals were suitable for herding.

column1: How Eurasia's domestic animals compared with the Americas'
column2: Eurasia had thirteen of the world's fourteen domesticated large mammals, while the Americas had only one, the llama and its relative the alpaca.
